Housekeeping
PRESIDENT:  Good morning, everybody.  This is the fifth day
of the evidentiary hearing in DIAC case no. 240079
between China State Construction Engineering Corporation
(Middle East) LLC and Dubai Integrated Economic Zones
Authority.
Before we turn to the evidence, I sent an email
yesterday wondering, bluntly, whether we can shave a day
or a bit of a day off the hearing.  Am I going to get
good news or bad news or "We don't know yet" news?
MS CHENG:  The parties have conferred, and I think
the difficulty is that we've all got our meetings with
experts for last-minute preparation scheduled in, and
both of us, I understand, would prefer to keep the
timetable as it is, with apologies to the tribunal.
PRESIDENT:  Right.  Well, the timetable is there and
we approved it, so I don't think we can order anything
different.
What might assist to try and finish on time on
Friday is a possible 9.30 start.  How would that go
down?  Like a lead balloon, or is that all right?
MS CHENG:  That works for us.
MR RIGNEY:  Us too.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, I mean, the other, I suppose, possibility,
is if quantum -- no, that's a bad point.
So we will carry on as before, but with a 9.30
start.
MS CHENG:  Sirs, we can confirm for my part.  I'm very
grateful for that, I do appreciate that.
PRESIDENT:  I understand.
MR RIGNEY:  Thank you very much.
PRESIDENT:  All right.
Now, that's the tribunal's housekeeping.  Ms Cheng,

MS CHENG:  Presentations: to be provided a day before.  May
I just ask -- I don't think we were specific about when
during that 24-hour period they're provided, but I think
we received ours at around midnight last night.  And the
tricky thing is my expert is to give evidence today, so
I suspect he got an early night, but it means that we
don't get an opportunity to consult until first thing in

earlier in the day, please?
MR RIGNEY:  Sir, I hadn't appreciated that that was the
position.  Ms Cheng is absolutely right: of course she
needs to get the presentations in good time.  And
I hope, Ms Cheng, that the message that you've just
conveyed has been heard by those sitting to my left.
I will ensure, or at least do the best that I can to
ensure, that you get the presentations in good time from
now on, because you're entirely right and that's
a perfectly fair complaint to make.
MS CHENG:  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  Is that the only issue of housekeeping?
MS CHENG:  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  Mr Rigney, anything from you?
MR RIGNEY:  Just to let you know, sir, that Mr Maxwell will
be cross-examining today.
PRESIDENT:  Right.  Good.  Thank you very much.
MR BILL HAGGART (continued)
PRESIDENT:  Right.  So you are still under the oath you took
yesterday, so we don't need to do that again.
Mr Maxwell, would you like to introduce the reports
and then we'll have the presentation.
MR MAXWELL:  Yes, sir.  Well, I introduced the three
individual reports by Mr Haggart yesterday, so I was
planning just to take him to the MEP joint statement and
also there's an additional errata, if that would be
convenient.
Examination-in-chief by MR MAXWELL
MR MAXWELL:  Mr Haggart, could we please have page {I4} up
on screen.
Is this a joint statement to which you contributed
with Dr Nigel Bish?
A.  Yes, it is.
Q.  Can we turn, please, to page 21.  Is that your signature
on the left-hand side?
A.  Yes, it is.
Q.  Could we now please turn to {I10}.  Is this
an additional errata sheet that was produced by you?
A.  It is indeed.
Q.  And is that your signature at the bottom?
A.  Yes, it is.
Q.  Is that joint statement, together with the documents to
which you were referred yesterday, and subject to the
errata sheets to which you referred yesterday and also
today, the evidence that you wish to provide in these
proceedings?
A.  Yes, it is.
Q.  And is that evidence a true and complete expression of
your professional opinion?
A.  It is indeed.
MR MAXWELL:  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  Well, Mr Haggart, you know the procedure.
Would you like to make your presentation.
WITNESS:  Yes, by all means.
Presentation by MR HAGGART
WITNESS:  I'd like to start my presentation by drawing your
attention to a slight error, which is on my behalf.
In the opening line of my presentation on the next
slide {I9-2}, where it refers briefly to the scope of
the work that I was instructed to undertake, you'll see
there a reference to "shop drawings process and general
progress of the works".  That has been included by error
and I do apologise.  So in case you are looking through
my reports for works relating to shop drawings process,
it's not there.  So just to tidy that up for you before
we move on, and please, please, do accept my apologies.
I mentioned to you yesterday that my reports
effectively are split into two sections: the media
facades we discussed at great length; and the second
section relates to, effectively, MEP issues, covering
defects and testing and commissioning.
My first report provides some analysis and summary
on alleged defective works in relation to earth pits and
earth rods, cove lighting, calorifiers, solar inverters,
external lighting, an issue with cracked pipes in the
lake pump room, chilled water pipework insulation, water
leaks in in-ground conduits and MSI works.  So a fairly
mixed basket of systems there.
My second report provides some further analysis in
response to some new issues raised by Dr Bish in his
first report in relation to testing and commissioning.
We then, Dr Bish and I, produced a joint statement
which summarises the areas of agreement and
disagreement.  And then subsequent to that, I produced
a third report, a shorter report, which responded to
some evidence introduced by Dr Bish during the joint
statement.
So that covers the ambit of the reports that are
produced.
Just to clarify, again, as yesterday, there is no
delay analysis done by me, or quantum analysis; at least
not in terms of pounds and pence.
If we move to the next slide, please.
One of the main features that came through in the
MEP reports are defects and issues associated with earth
pits and earth rods.  In summary, the genesis of this
issue arose -- DIEZA was informed that there was
a problem with some high earthing readings, and were
instructed to investigate and look at the cause of some
high earth values.  And during the course of this work,
some issues relating to water in the earth pits and some
broken or damaged earth rods were uncovered during
the course of the investigations, and I've attached
there -- you'll see this in my report, that describes
those findings.
Just to set the scene for you, in case you're not
familiar with earth rods and earth pits and all
the components that go with that.
The black and white or the grey figure in the middle
of this slide is a very simple diagram showing
a cross-section of a typical earth rod installation, and
what you see there, if you go from top to bottom, is
what we call the earth pit.  Now, that can be either
a concrete box or a high-density plastic box.  It's with
a lid, it goes over the top, and it protects the box
underneath from water ingress and dust ingress and
general tampering and interference.
And inside that box, you see the top of what is
the earth rod, which is -- it's not a very sophisticated
piece of equipment.  It's effectively a long copper rod
which is bolted together in sections, and driven into
the ground or inserted into a borehole into the ground
to make a solid connection to earth.  That earth rod is
then connected at the top, inside the pit, with a cable,
and that cable finds its way back through a conduit
system or a ducting system back to the main electrical
switchgear to provide the earthing connection.
One of the location-specific aspects of the earthing
installation is that if the ground is not particularly
conductive, things have to be done to make it
conductive.  And there's a compound often and commonly
used in the industry, called bentonite, that basically
gets mixed up and poured into the hole that the earth
rod goes into, to create a more conductive connection to
earth.  And that's the darker grey outline you can see
around that earth rod.
And that's effectively it.  It's not a very
sophisticated or complicated installation or system,
when you look at it from that diagram.
Where it does get a little bit complicated is in
the actual sealing of the earth pit and the earth rod
against groundwater.  So every building is built on
ground and there's a water table in it, and that water
table is at different heights.  Now, that's not my area
of expertise, the geological aspects of water tables and
how high they are or how low they are.  But what we must
do is protect the earth pit from ingress of that water
coming up through the ground, and filling up the earth
pit from the bottom up.
So the detail of the construction of the earth pits
is shown on the diagram on the right-hand side there.
And what that shows -- perhaps if I could ask if
we could zoom in on that diagram on the right; there's
quite a bit of detail there.
While that's happening, I'll talk through what's
there.
Effectively, there's a double-seal system.  Because
what happens is that the concrete slab in the basement
of a building has to be penetrated by the earth rod in
order for it to get to the depth it needs to get to to
make contact with earth, and that penetration goes
through the concrete and it goes through the
waterproofing membrane, which is part of the structural
detailing, and all that has to be sealed.
So you can see what's called a "Membrane seal":
it's a two-sided clamp which effectively seals off the
penetration.  And again, there's another seal inside the
earth rod.  So should anything come up through there,
there's a second barrier, if you will.
The other aspect to this is when a rod is being
driven through a concrete slab, there's a sleeve that
gets -- a sleeve is put in place, it's inserted to give
it a conduit, and you can see that conduit there in
cross-section that the rod is driven through.
So these are the complicated parts of the earthing
system, the sealing of the earth pit from
the groundwater that can rise up.
If we can zoom back out again, please.
And just in terms of -- again, just to give you
the context, I've provided a short summary of the
specification.  There is much more detail on that in
my reports.  Effectively, there was a specification
requirement that the earth pits were to be sealed
against water ingress and the earth rods were to be
a minimum length of 2.4m.  So that gives you an idea of
the depth that these rods have to be driven into the
ground for the lightning protection system, and for the
electrical earthing system, it was specified to be 6m.
So these are effectively two different earthing
systems, with unique rods for each system.  Ultimately
they all get connected back to earth, in the grand
scheme of things, but as installations they are separate
systems.
And the performance requirements, if you like, of
each of these earthing systems was that the lightning
protection system had to be less than 10 ohms -- ohms is
the measure of resistance to earth -- and for the
electrical installation to be less than 1 ohm.  These
are important figures because -- this is where we delve
into electrical engineering theory a little bit, because
the lower the resistance to earth, which is what we're
trying to achieve, the higher the fault current that is
generated under a fault condition.
That might sound a little bit counterintuitive, but
a high fault current is needed to instantly disconnect
the protective breakers back at the main switchboards.
So if the earth resistance is higher, then the earth
fault current is lower, and it takes longer to activate
the circuit protectors, the circuit-breakers.
Now, we're talking about the differences of
milliseconds in the operation of these breakers, but it
is important in the context of risk of electric shock
and health and safety to the users, because the
difference in milliseconds could be the difference, dare
I say, between life and death in extreme circumstances.
So I hope that gives you an appreciation of
the technology and the specification.
If we could move to the next slide, please.
So one of the issues is these earth pits were filled
with water.  I saw that.  I visited site, I looked at
a handful of earth pits, and it wasn't just a splash of
water in the bottom; they were filled almost to
the brim, filled with water.
Just going back to the detail of the earth pits.  So
you can see the photograph there.  What is not very
clear from that photograph is how deep the water is, or
how high up.  But please take my word for it: there was
a lot of water in the earth pits.
Now, in our reports and in our joint statement, you
will see some discussion between Dr Bish and I about
the waterproofing qualities of the lids, the thing on
top of the earth pit, and we both agree they're not
designed specifically to be watertight.  They don't have
what we call an ingress protection routing associated
with them.  The lids though, they're a very tightly
fitting lid.
The cross-section you can see there may not be
obvious, so I'll try and explain it to you.  Perhaps if
we can zoom in on that a little bit.
While that's happening, you can see in the
photograph, you can see four holes on the lid, which is
the kind of square piece of equipment with the yellow
piece of paint on it.  You can see four holes.  These
are holes that contain holding-down bolts.  So the lid
is physically screwed into the casing of the earth pit.
So you do have a gap around the top of the earth
pit.  Now, that gap is just inside -- if you can look at
the diagram, you'll see a dimension at the top, second
top: 256mm.  And if you just go inside the extremities
of that dimension, that's the extent of the lid.  And
that lid, it's not just a flat lid, it's on kind of
legs, and those legs sit on a ledge inside the actual
pit itself.  So even if water does trickle in through
the very small gap at the top, it kind of gets stopped
at the point where the lid meets the ledge.
Of course there will be a possible route for some
water to find its way into the earth pit from the top,
but it's my view that it's highly unlikely that any
water of that volume would have found its way into the
earth pits, even if somebody had poured a bucket of
water on top.  Some would have gone through.
If we can zoom back out, please.
So I mentioned in the first slide, or described,
rather, the waterproofing aspects to protect against
groundwater.  And the project record shows that during
the works, the issue of groundwater seepage, ie water
coming up through the ground into the earth pits, was
known, and I've made some reference there and you'll
find that in my report.
More so you'll find in the project record that
chemical injection works were proposed by China State in
April 2019 and 2020 to the earth pits to make them
waterproof.  That says to me that that problem was
known.  There was a course of action identified to
remedy, or attempt to remedy, the water ingress.  And
chemical injection is a fairly intrusive process: it
effectively involves a bit of excavation and pumping
chemical sealant into the system to plug any gaps.
I don't really have too many examples that I can
give you that would -- I used the example yesterday of
buying a TV in John Lewis.  I mean, if you have central
heating at home, the closest analogy I could probably
give you is: if your central heating is leaking, the
pipework, you would pour some chemical sealant into
the pipework which effectively plugs the holes.  It's
not the same, but it's that kind of process: we're
pumping something into the system to remedy leaks or
defects in the membranes that allow the water to come
through into the earth pits.
As I've said, surface water coming from the top
going in is of course another possibility of water
ingress, but it's highly unlikely, in my opinion, that
to that extent that would occur.  During my visit, when
I had the walk-round with DIEZA's FM team, they
explained to me that even after going through a process
of dewatering -- so there was dewatering process where
the water was taken out -- that it had come back again,
and this was during a period of no rain, dry weather,
and in the absence of any water-based cleaning
activities.
So while there are a number of -- well, there are
probably two main routes or options for water getting
into the earth pits, either through the top or up
through the bottom, it remains my opinion that this is
water that's come from groundwater rising up, high water
table.
If we go to the next slide, please.
So I mentioned at the start, the other issue that
was uncovered during the investigation into the
earthworks was that some of the earth rods were actually
damaged.  And you'll see in some of the witness evidence
that some sections of earth rods were lying loose,
connected to a 1m-long or less piece of copper earth
rod.
I've provided this diagram here.  This is an extract
from the supplier's literature: it shows how an earth
rod is actually built up and constructed.  It's sections
of copper rod.  They're bolted together by what's called
a coupling dowel.  That's a physically screwed-together
mechanism.  At the bottom, you'll see there's a spike:
that's the sharp end, to allow it to be driven into the
ground.  And at the top, there's what's called the
driving stud, and that's the thing that gets hit with
a percussion hammer to drive the spike into the ground.
These sections come in stock lengths of 1.2m or 3m
or 5m.  One of the discussions that Dr Bish and I had,
was: how were these sections of earth rod that were
uncovered less than 1m?  And I don't know the answer to
that.  I've got a theory.  But when you get an earth rod
and you drive it into the ground, at some point it can
go no further, and there may well be a large piece of
earth rod sticking up beyond the top of the earth pit
and it has to be cut off.  But that's simply a theory.
I can't explain why sections of rod less than the stock
length of 1.2m were discovered.
The other thing that I should bring to your
attention is: we saw the specified insertion depths of
2.4m and 6m.  Some of these rods were actually driven in
to depths of 10m, and that's usual, that's normal,
depending on, during the testing, if they were getting
appropriate earth resistance readings -- if the reading
isn't appropriate, they would drive another section of
rod until they got something that was adequate.
Now, you could not, one could not -- nobody in this
room, I would suspect, could manually lift that 10m-long
or 6m-long or even 2.4m-long rod out of the ground once
it's been driven into the ground.  It would be, in
simple terms, like trying to manually pull out a nail
that's been hammered into a piece of wood.  It just
should not be able to happen.
Loose connections.  I've said already that these are
fairly simply installations.  There should be no loose
connections on the earth rod, and there's no real
natural wear and tear from normal maintenance activities
that would cause any loosening of sections of the earth
rod once they're in.
We mentioned the chemical injection works
previously, and I've put a photograph there that shows
some excavation around an earth pit.  That excavation
would have required jackhammers and all sorts of heavy
industrial machinery to break through the concrete slab.
Now, if anything caused any earth rod to break or become
damaged, it is my opinion that that's the obvious
candidate.
If we move to the next slide, please.
So a very different topic now: cove lighting.
This is something that appears in the partial defects
liability certificate.  Cove lighting, again,
I witnessed a couple of times during my walk-round on
site, and you can see the photograph top left there is
a photograph I took.
So the cove lighting, these are LED strips that are
built into architectural features.  It's intended to
give a very continuous, floating effect to the ceiling.
It's very much an architectural feature.  And these
strips are cut to various lengths and sizes to suit
the installation.
In my review of the taking-over certificate snag
lists, I identified that there were over 100 defects
that had been listed in relation to cove lighting.  As
I say, the cove lighting issue was still there in the
defects liability certificate.
This is not something that Dr Bish addresses in his
report, so you don't have anything to compare.  But the
purpose of the cove lighting really is -- it's a linear
system: it should be uniform in appearance and then
colour.  There shouldn't be any of these dark spots that
you see in that photograph.  And it's a key
architectural feature of the building, so a fairly
important part of the lighting installation.
Naturally, of course, LEDs will fail over time.  But
LEDs, unlike conventional lightbulbs, have a very
unusual characteristic.  Some of them will fail within
a few hours of installation.  Most of them, once they
get past that few hours of installation, go on for many,
many years of operation.  And you may know that yourself
from even your own domestic situation, if you've got LED
lighting at home.
But there was a high number of these snags recorded
in the snag lists: it suggests that it was a widespread
issue.
I made a reference in my reports to two other
reports provided by the China State supplier of the
LEDs, who cite incorrect wiring, incorrect installation
and damage to the LEDs that were supplied, and that
would be consistent with the failure in the light.
These are fairly -- they're LED lights, not dissimilar
to the LEDs we talked about yesterday, but they're more
flexible, they're more fragile, they have to bend around
corners.  And so installation is very important, or care
in installation is very important.
If we move to the next slide, please.
Another issue that arises are defects in calorifiers
in the hotel building.  The calorifiers are effectively
hot water storage tanks.  They contain a heating element
that heats the water so that it's available on demand in
the hotel.  And they're standard pieces of equipment in
commercial buildings.
Five of them, I understand, were installed in
the hotel building for the hot water provision for
the catering and guest facilities.  From correspondence,
I understand that the leaks were first reported by
the hotel staff in April 2021, and the email refers to
shortly after handover.
There's a strange course of action where an attempt
was made by the operator or DIEZA to rectify the leak on
one of the calorifiers by a weld, which failed.  It was
tried and it was stopped; it didn't work.
The other issue in regards to the calorifiers is
that the installer, Ecoval, states that it's no longer
the agent for the manufacturer -- sorry, not the
installer, the provider -- and the manufacturer, which
is an Italian company, Caldaie, says that the warranty
issue lies with Ecoval.  So there appears to have been
some kind of impasse there between the manufacturer and
the supplier which meant that the defects weren't being
addressed by these parties.
Ecoval subsequently visited the site, and their
report identified that the failures of the leaks in the
calorifiers were the result of improper maintenance
and/or disconnected anodes, and I'll explain that
a little bit.
The anodes in this case are an active component:
they are an electrical component which sit inside the
calorifiers.  They change the electrochemical balance in
the water, and their primary purpose is to reduce the
potential for corrosion inside the calorifiers.
If they're not there, it doesn't mean that the
calorifiers are going to start rusting the next day once
they're switched off.  What it would mean, in my view,
is that the calorifiers, that are expected to have
a lifespan of maybe, say, 25 years, would probably start
to fail in 20 years: they wouldn't reach their full
lifespan.  They would not start to crumble or
deteriorate in such a short space of time.  It just
wouldn't be normal.  Even the absence of proper
maintenance -- and I'm not saying that there wasn't any
proper maintenance.  But these calorifiers are steel
tanks: they don't just collapse in such a short period
of time.
Now, there were two other reports done which I think
kind of get to the nub of the issue really, and these
are explained in some detail in my reports.
Avotech, in March 2023, identified cold cracks in
the tanks adjacent to where welding connections were
made.  And I think it might be helpful to zoom in on
that photograph, top right, please.  What you can see
there, circled in red, these are the cold cracks that
are referred to in the report.
Now, I'm by no means a welding expert, but I do
understand terms such as "stress cracking" and "cold
cracking".  I did do a small welding course at
Strathclyde University 35 years ago, but that's the
extent of it.  This is not corrosion caused by water;
this is completely different.  This is where the metal
has been stressed and cracked.
PRESIDENT:  Speaking for myself, I can't really see what
I'm supposed to see in the upper and righter of the
two ...
WITNESS:  All that you can see, if you really look in
closely, you will see what looks like lightning fronds
coming away from a central piece.  And that's very, very
typical of stress cracking.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
WITNESS:  And another report -- sorry, thanks, if we could
go back and zoom back out.
Another report done by a company called FLIR,
they did a thermography inspection, which is effectively
a heat check on the metal casing, which identified some
defects in the welding.
So both conclusions mention deformities in
the structure of the steel or manufacturing defects or
welding defects.
It's my view that any leaks that sprung from these
calorifiers were not as a result of any apparent lack of
maintenance or disconnection of anodes, not so quickly
after handover.  Leaks do appear, but they appear at
jointed connections, so when pipes are connected to
equipment and perhaps a gasket isn't properly bolted
together, or the bolts aren't tight enough, then leaks
appear.  But that's a very easy remedy to fix that leak.
Leaks that come from structural damage in the casing,
this is a different thing, in my view.
If we go to the next slide, please.
Chilled water pipework insulation.  I think you
heard some evidence already on this from the fact
witnesses.  I mean, there's a fundamental requirement
that all the chilled water pipeworks and the support
systems are fully and properly insulated.
It's recorded in my report, there are photographs of
areas where that has not been the case: there have been
gaps in the installation of the insulation.  And when
that happens, warm, humid air gets into the pipework.
It condenses.  It can travel anywhere inside the
pipework by capillary action.  It then accumulates and
starts to drip through the insulation.
You can see in the photograph there, it's not very
clear, but that is typical of the staining you would get
on the underside of pipework that has condensation drips
falling through, the staining.  And the reason it's
stained is there are many different soluble aspects in
the chilled water pipework.
First of all, the pipe itself, I haven't seen the
detail, but usually they're either painted or covered in
some kind of polymer.  There's an adhesive wrapping
underneath the insulation.  The insulation itself is
covered in this white material, which is effectively
an adhesive wrap painted with an anti-fungal emulsion,
and that's a typical insulation.
So you have water passing through these things,
they're going to pick up solubles in these applications,
and this is why we sometimes see this -- we see
the staining.  And if that water then drips on these
solubles, it will more than likely stain whatever
it lands on underneath.
Dr Bish and I agree on an awful lot in regards to
the chilled water pipework insulation, and we agree that
whatever has been done to rectify that has been a good
job and it's rectified the condensation issues.
If we go to the next slide, please.
The master system integrator works, the MSI works.
This is a topic that appears in my first report; it's
not responded to by Dr Bish.  And the essence of this,
my opinion really was to give some opinion on how the
MSI works related to other MEP systems, and whether
testing and commissioning could proceed while the MSI
works remained ongoing and incomplete.
So the MSI works themselves, this is the specialist
works that link all of the systems in all of the
buildings together back to a central command and control
point over what's called a VLAN, a virtual local area
network.  This is the IT network, and the VLAN is the
software that sits on top of that, and that's unique and
specific to the user.  Many of these VLANs are top
secret; the programming of IP addresses are codes that
are unique to the operator.
So while the MSI works integrate all these systems
together back to a common command and control point,
each building is a standalone entity that can be tested
and commissioned, because each building has its own BMS
system, its own control systems for lighting and so on,
fire alarms.  All these systems can be tested
individually.  And when they're all connected back to
the central command point, it gives the user a common
interface where they can look at each building together.
So two separate things.  I think maybe the best way
to think of it is that you don't need the MSI works to
allow the buildings to operate fully and function fully,
in terms of the MEP systems and the testing and
commissioning.  All of that VLAN work requires cables,
pieces of hardware called routers and switches, and
an element of programming to bring it all together.
One of the things I was asked to consider was if it
would be feasible to allocate temporary IP addresses.
Now, this is a programming issue, so it's not really my
sphere of expertise, but I am familiar with the
technology and I know that IP addresses are simply
numbers that are programmed in, so it would be feasible
to allocate IP addresses on a temporary basis.
If we could move to the next slide, please.
Testing and commissioning.  Testing and
commissioning is something Dr Bish introduced to me in
his report, which I responded to.  And what I've done is
really addressed this as the key question of: was all
the testing and commissioning done by the end of
